newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader, vilified in West, loved at home.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader, vilified in West, loved at home.

text.p: Not many leaders could dismiss the elected parliament, clamp down on press freedom, sign away the nation's independence, preside over economic stagnation, find something positive to say about Adolf Hitler and still remain popular.
But Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, who signed a Union Treaty with Russia's Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday, has managed it.
The former Communist Party activist is loathed by nationalists in his small former Soviet republic and regularly denounced by the West for his human rights record.
But his simple, populist rhetoric has won him the hearts of Belarussian voters and the respect of many Russians as well. He is only 42 and some analysts see his ultimate goal as the Kremlin.

The former state farm boss swept to power in 1994 on a platform of fighting corruption and renewing ties with Moscow. Coming from behind, he easily won the election, defeating opinion poll favourites.

Since then, Lukshenko has used strong-arm tactics to clamp down on the nationalist opposition, kept Russian-style market reforms at bay and won backing from both the Russian opposition and the Kremlin in his drive for a closer union with Moscow.
Shrugging off international criticism, he won a landslide victory last November in a referendum to rewrite the constitution and vastly increase his powers.
Supporters call the lean, angular, moustachioed leader "father". Opponents compare him to Hitler and Benito Mussolini.

In 1995, in an interview with a German newspaper, Lukashenko praised Hitler's strong rule in pre-war Germany -- this from the leader of a country one-quarter of whose population died during the 1941-4 Nazi occupation.
Yet Belarussians apparently like his direct style.

During a telephone conference with regional leaders, broadcast across the country of 10 million last week to mark the start of the spring sowing campaign, Lukashenko accused the Minsk regional governor of trying to deceive him.
"Tell me how you tried to pull the wool over the president's eyes and washed cows with shampoo when I was planning to visit two districts of our region," he railed.
He also vowed to ensure the campaign -- agriculture is still state-run -- went to plan by surprising farmers in his helicopter, a present from Yeltsin.
Lukashenko sometimes coopts the state television to address the nation in a didactic tone, slamming senior officials, for up to three hours at a time.
Prime Minister Sergei Ling, reporting to top officials in February, got a tongue-lashing when he announced that monthly inflation had leapt to 13.3 percent in January.
"I am hearing for the first time that you have not fulfilled the programme. You have failed me!" shouted Lukashenko, who had decreed that average prices should grow by only two percent a month.
Some analysts put Lukashenko's popularity down to the fact that the population is relatively elderly and misses the Soviet Union -- a nostalgia on which he often plays.

Belarus has failed to establish a strong national identity during five years of independence -- most people still prefer Russian to the local tongue -- and Lukashenko exploits this. He has banned the display of red-and-white nationalist symbols, replacing them with Soviet-era ones.
Despite the noisy opposition and a clamour of criticism in the West especially from Washington, Lukashenko is unchallenged in Belarus.
His attitude to foreign visitors led a group of European officials who met him last year to describe their conversation as "two monologues". He once called NATO a monster.

Alexander Grigoryevich Lukashenko was born in the village of Kopys in eastern Belarus. In Soviet days he was a "politruk" or political instructor in the Soviet Army and a low-level activist in the Komsomol youth organisation.
